mstts:express-as.prosody: Welcome in—let’s take a moment to really look at the world around us, and ask: how do power, sexuality, and desire shape the ways we live and relate to one another? Sometimes, these forces are so deeply woven into our everyday lives that we barely notice them, even though they’re influencing everything from our relationships to the stories we see and hear. Together, we’re about to step into some challenging territory—guided by Andrea Dworkin’s fearless work, Pornography: Men Possessing Women. In her writing, Dworkin doesn’t just point out what’s on the surface. She invites us to dig deeper, to question how the commodification of women’s bodies isn’t just happening by accident, but is actually a powerful mechanism that keeps patriarchal control alive and well. What if pornography isn’t just a matter of personal choice or private fantasy? What if it’s a cultural force, shaping how we see gender, what we think consent means, and even how violence is justified? As we explore, we’ll see how the relentless objectification of women becomes so normal, so everyday, that it can feel invisible—hidden behind the language of freedom and fantasy. Dworkin’s analysis doesn’t just skim the surface. She pushes us to reconsider the very foundation of our ideas about desire, agency, and what it means to be free. And along the way, she asks us to really think: what does it cost us, as a society, when possession is mistaken for pleasure? So, as we move forward, let’s be curious—and let’s be honest with ourselves. Because in these questions, the stakes couldn’t be higher: we’re talking about the very terms on which we define our own humanity.
